title: Nash Equilibria in Constrained Games
one_liner: When multiple players each optimize their own choices but share a common constraint, a fair deal exists where no one wants to switch.
lead: Imagine two trucking companies routing deliveries through the same city—each wants to minimize its own costs, but both must obey a city-wide fuel cap. Does a fair deal exist where both companies find their routes acceptable and neither wants to cheat? The paper proves yes under natural conditions, and gives an algorithm to find it.

paras: In real problems, multiple independent players compete or cooperate, each trying to optimize their own goals. Trucking companies minimize fuel cost. Traders minimize portfolio risk. Wireless networks maximize signal strength. The catch: they share a common resource or rule. Total fuel used across all trucks cannot exceed the city budget. Total trading volume cannot flood the market. Total radio power cannot exceed the FCC limit.

A beginner might hope each player can ignore the others and optimize alone—plug in the constraint and compute. But that breaks immediately: if one player bends the constraint to favor themselves, others lose their fair share. If all players optimize in isolation without coordinating, they often violate the shared rule or end up with an outcome where someone has a strong incentive to cheat. No stable deal emerges.

callout.html: Prove a fair outcome exists where all players find their choices acceptable and the shared constraint holds (because fixed point theory guarantees it), then use an algorithm that nudges each player's choices toward higher rewards while a soft penalty pushes back if they approach the constraint boundary.

panels.title: 1. Each player wants to optimize alone
panels.caption: Five trucks each choose their own route to minimize fuel cost.

panels.title: 2. But there is a shared budget
panels.caption: All trucks must share one city fuel limit; violate it and no one operates.

panels.title: 3. Each truck negotiates its share
panels.caption: Two trucks adjust routes down; three stay put. The constraint is satisfied.

panels.title: 4. Is this a fair deal?
panels.viz_args: Nash equilibrium: no truck wants to deviate
panels.caption: Each truck gets an acceptable route share; none benefits from alone switching.

panels.title: 5. The algorithm converges to it
panels.caption: An uphill-walking process guided by a barrier finds the fair outcome step by step.

steps.b: Start with a feasible starting point
steps.text: Initialize all players' strategies so the shared constraint is not violated.

steps.b: Measure each player's incentive to move
steps.text: Find which direction would improve each player's goal if they moved, because moving toward higher rewards makes sense only if it makes you better off.

steps.b: Add a soft wall at the boundary
steps.text: A log barrier method gently penalizes strategies that approach the constraint limit, so the algorithm avoids overshooting.
Move each player in the direction of higher rewards, but scale the step size differently: bigger steps when there is slack, smaller when near the edge.

steps.b: Repeat until no one wants to move
steps.text: Stop when the incentives for all players to move further shrink close to zero, signaling an acceptable deal has been found.

paras: The paper identifies and updates the players' strategies (their action choices—routes, trades, power levels—and how much of the shared constraint each one uses) until all players agree no unilateral move helps them, because once no one wants to switch unilaterally, the deal is stable and no player needs to worry about being cheated.

hidden.name: Distance to constraint violation
paras: The algorithm secretly tracks how close each player is to overshooting their share of the constraint. This distance is invisible in the problem statement, but it drives the algorithm's pacing: if a player has plenty of slack, the algorithm can take a larger step. If a player is already near the limit, smaller steps keep them safe.

The log barrier method estimates this distance and uses it to add a penalty when strategies drift toward the boundary, because a penalty that grows as you approach the edge naturally steers you away from breaking the shared rule. The algorithm then measures progress by watching how this margin shrinks and stabilizes: a vanishing margin signals an acceptable deal has been found.

heat.caption: Darker means more unused share in the constraint budget; lighter means player is near their limit.

reads.html: Imagine a tank with 100 gallons for five trucks. If one truck uses 40, it has 60 gallons to go. If another has used 50, it has 50 left. The algorithm watches how much slack each truck has and takes smaller steps as it approaches empty, because a smaller step keeps you safer when you are close to running out.

The log barrier method encodes the constraint as a soft penalty that grows as strategies approach the boundary of the allowed region. This penalty pushes back harder the closer you get, so strategies naturally stay safe. The algorithm uses this margin information to pick adaptive stepsizes: bigger steps when there is slack, smaller steps when margin is tight.

paras: Each player is trying to improve their own goal (minimize cost, maximize profit) by moving their strategy in the direction of steepest ascent. But they cannot move freely—the shared constraint sits like a wall. The log barrier method builds a soft penalty that pushes back as any player nears the wall; the strength of the pushback increases the closer you get. This works like a spring: far from the edge it is relaxed, but as you approach it gets stiffer, redirecting players away from forbidden moves without locking them in place.

The adaptive stepsize then lets the algorithm be bold when there is plenty of room and cautious when any player is near the edge, because big steps when you have slack get closer to a good solution faster, while tiny steps when you are near the edge keep you safe. As all players nudge their strategies forward in parallel, the shared constraint stays satisfied, and their desires to move further (measured by how strongly their incentives pull them toward higher rewards) gradually shrink. When all incentives reach near-zero, no player wants to switch unilaterally—a stable deal has been found, and the algorithm stops.

The reason existence holds: under playerwise concavity, the set of all valid strategy combinations has special properties that fixed point theory exploits—a mathematical result that guarantees a fair deal exists somewhere. The algorithm then finds it by moving uphill on this well-structured space.

stages.s: Find which direction improves each player's goal, because moving that direction is how you chase better rewards
Apply log barrier: add penalty near constraint boundary
Adjust stepsize: move boldly when slack is high, cautiously when low
Update all players' strategies in parallel
Stable deal: no player wants to deviate alone

math.words: Each player updates their strategy by moving in the direction of their goal plus a term that penalizes getting too close to the constraint limit. The penalty strength depends on how far the log of the remaining slack is from infinity, scaled by a barrier coefficient.
symbols: direction to improve each player's objective
weight on the constraint penalty (how hard the wall pushes back)
how the penalty changes as you move toward the boundary

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Truck 1: current cost gradient is 0.8 units/step, barrier gradient is 0.1 units (penalty as it nears the fuel limit). Net movement: 0.8 - (1.0 × 0.1) = 0.7 units.
Truck 2: cost gradient is 0.5, but it is close to its fuel limit, so barrier gradient is 0.4. Net movement: 0.5 - (1.0 × 0.4) = 0.1 units (it moves cautiously).
Truck 3: cost gradient is 0.9, barrier gradient is 0.05 (plenty of slack). Net movement: 0.9 - (1.0 × 0.05) = 0.85 units. Bold move because slack is high. All three stay feasible.

math.note: The barrier penalty acts like a spring that softly repels players from violating the constraint because the penalty grows (and thus pushes back harder) as you approach the boundary, while the uphill direction across their goal directs them toward better outcomes.

charts.title: Naive approach (no coordination)
charts.note: Each player optimizes alone, violates the shared rule, and someone wants to deviate.

charts.title: This paper (barrier-based algorithm)
charts.note: All players reach better goals than the naive approach, the constraint is always honored because the barrier penalty steers strategies away from the boundary, and no one has an incentive to cheat because their incentives to move have shrunk to near-zero.

items.html: If a player's goal is concave (curves downward like a valley) but the constraint is not, the fixed-point argument breaks, and equilibrium may not exist. The paper requires playerwise concavity, which is a real constraint.

If the penalty weight is too low, the algorithm ignores the constraint and strays infeasible, because a weak penalty is easily overridden by the goal-improvement direction. If it is too high, the algorithm gets stuck in the penalty and never improves goals, because the push-back from the barrier becomes so strong that no uphill movement is allowed. Finding the sweet spot is a tuning burden.

items.b: Convergence is slow for high precision.
items.html: The algorithm's cost grows as roughly epsilon to the power of minus three to reach an acceptable solution with error smaller than epsilon, meaning tiny improvements near the goal take many iterations. For highly accurate answers, this cost grows fast.

items.b: With perfect information and adaptive stepsizes, convergence is guaranteed.
items.html: The algorithm finds an equilibrium provably if players can measure their objectives perfectly and the stepsize adapts correctly. In practice, noisy measurements or fixed stepsizes can hurt.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple two-player game: players choose spending amounts to maximize a reward that depends on both choices, subject to a shared total-spending cap. Run the barrier algorithm and a naive independent-optimization baseline. Plot each player's objective over iterations and track whether the shared constraint is obeyed. The demo should show the barrier algorithm converging to a feasible, stable outcome where neither player wants to unilaterally deviate, while the naive method violates the constraint and leaves players unsatisfied.
demo.closing: The demo must make plain that the barrier algorithm keeps the shared constraint honored because the log barrier penalty repels strategies away from the boundary, while also converging to outcomes where all players agree no individual deviation helps, proving the algorithm's core promise.
